newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: "Vindictive" PNG government sacks army rebel.
newsitem.headline: "Vindictive" PNG government sacks army rebel.

text.p: The Papua New Guinea army chief who led a military revolt in March against Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan for hiring African mercenaries has been thrown out of the defence force by Chan's dying government.
Chan's cabinet, which has suffered major defeats in the current election because of the mercenary deal, decommissioned Brigadier General Jerry Singirok last week.
The dismissal was announced in a government gazette on Thursday, but no reason was given.
Chan's government is in disarray, with 15 ministers including Chan himself losing their seats in the election.
Counting will end on July 15 and a new government, which is not expected to include Chan's party, will be announced at the end of the month.
Singirok, who had already been sacked by Chan as army chief, said on Thursday his decommissioning was an act of vindictiveness by the politicians he had brought down.

"The actions by this government to terminate my commission after having revoked my appointment as the commander of the PNG Defence Force without giving me reasons is unjust and can only be interpreted as vindictiveness," Singirok said.
"This violates all principles of natural justice. I am not a criminal as I acted for the interest of this nation."
Singirok, who has been in the army for 20 years including the last four as commander, indicated he will take legal action against his sacking from the force.
Opposition leader Roy Yaki said Singirok's dismissal would only hamper attempts to restore stability to the South Pacific nation's defence force.
Yaki accused Chan and his deputy Chris Haiveta, who has retained his seat, of trying to "settle the score" before a new government is formed.
"Out of their desire to take revenge, these two men are adding further fuel to the fire," Yaki said.

Chan secretly hired 70-odd African mercenaries in January from the British military consultancy Sandline International to end the nine-year-old secessionist rebellion on the resource-rich island of Bougainville.
Singirok led an army revolt against the move, plunging the nation into its worst crisis since independence in 1975.
The revolt led to two days of looting in the capital Port Moresby and forced Chan to step aside pending a judicial inquiry into the US$36 million mercenary deal.

Chan returned to office just before the election after the injuiry failed to find any corruption in the deal. But the political backlash by voters against the mercenaries and Chan has seen severe and widespread.
